What do you think happened when this Yukon river lost most of its water in just four days?
Would you have noticed it was gone if you lived near Kluane Lake?

comments.author: @ER-yu2kd
comments.text: My family visited the lake in the 90s for a road trip to Alaska. We took a helicopter ride to see the glacier. Visiting it is a fond family memory, it was beautiful, serene and remote - wild.  The colour was spectacular.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: That sounds like an incredible family memory. Seeing the glacier from a helicopter in the 90s must have been something else, especially in a place as remote as Kluane. I can only imagine how spectacular the lake looked from the air. Thanks for sharing this, memories like these really add to the story.

comments.author: @joesutherland225
comments.text: Chum? that far up river? Odd everywhere I know of they are the species that spawn close to the ocean pinks as well. You sure it's chum and not Chinook?

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Good question, I double-checked this one because that migration distance does sound surprising. It is fall chum, not Chinook. The upper Yukon chum are unusual compared with many southern populations, some travel more than 2,700 km upriver, and the Kluane River is a documented spawning area. They may actually make one of the longest chum salmon migrations in the world. Pretty incredible fish.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: I appreciate the correction, especially from people who know the area. 👍

replies.author: @kseltl
replies.text: ​@HiddenCanadaI dont live there  currently lived there 2020-2025 it's a amazing place

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Yeah, that’s one of the biggest changes people around Kluane have had to live with since the river shifted. The exposed silt from the old riverbed can get picked up by the wind and turn into huge dust storms. They happened before 2016 too, but uncovering that much extra sediment made the problem a lot worse. Thanks for adding the local perspective.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Thanks, my friend! One of the wildest parts of this story is that the drainage really has changed naturally before. But for the 2016 event, researchers were actually able to track what happened pretty closely, glacier retreat opened a steeper route south, and the river was captured in just four days. Nature can rearrange a landscape incredibly fast.
